title: Codes that fix themselves
summary: Bits flip in memory, cables and disks. A parity bit finds a flip, a checksum finds any change, and Hamming codes find which bit flipped and flip it back.

text: XOR, ^ in $(( )), gives 1 when an odd number of its bits are 1. A parity bit is the XOR of the data: with it, the word always holds an even number of 1s.
- On arrival, XOR every bit: 0 means fine, 1 means a bit flipped.
- It can't tell which bit, and two flips cancel out: 0 again.
- | is OR, not XOR: 1 | 1 = 1, so it can't count.

scheme: one bit flips on the disk
sha256sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT
text: A checksum plays the role of parity for a whole file: sha256sum turns it into 64 hex digits, and one flipped bit changes almost all of them.
- It detects, it doesn't repair: on FAILED, download or copy the file again.
- Downloads publish such a file (Debian's SHA256SUMS). Against tampering, not just noise, it must be signed too: gpg --verify.
- On macOS, without coreutils: shasum -a 256 -c backup.sha256.

scheme: holds      p1 p2 d1 p4 d2 d3 d4
text: Hamming(7,4) sends 4 data bits (d) with 3 parity bits (p), each the XOR of a different group of positions.
- Check k reads the positions whose binary number includes k: 5 is 101 = 4 + 1, so s1 and s4 read it.
- No two positions are read by the same set of checks: that's what lets the checks point at one.
On arrival, compute the three checks again. Read as a binary number s4 s2 s1, they give the position that flipped: 0 means none.
- Flip that bit back, b[bad] ^ 1, then keep positions 3, 5, 6 and 7: the data.
- One flip is fixed; two point at the wrong bit. ECC RAM adds one overall parity bit (8 check bits per 64): it fixes one flip and detects two.
